chunks: What happens when a clock is too fast. The question: What happens if a clock is too fast?
Every clock tick gives the logic a fixed amount of time to finish its work.
If you speed the clock up so the next tick arrives before the slowest logic is done, the circuit captures an unfinished answer.
You get wrong results, often only for certain inputs.
A baker pulls a tray out of the oven on a fixed timer. Most items bake in 10 minutes, but the thick loaf needs 20.
Set the timer to 15 minutes and the rolls come out fine while the loaf comes out raw. A chip behaves the same way: the slowest path fails first.
Heat or a lower supply voltage slows every path, so a clock that works on a cool day can fail on a hot one.
As the available time shrinks (clock gets faster), the fraction of failing paths climbs from essentially zero to nearly all.
A design that is marginal fails some paths first, which is why failures start sporadically and then become systematic.
(A logistic curve is used here as a smooth stand-in for a Gaussian delay distribution.)
Clock period: the time between ticks, which is 1 divided by the clock frequency. Critical path: the slowest chain of logic between two flip-flops (one-bit memories).
It sets the fastest safe clock. Slack: spare time on a path, equal to the period minus the time the path needs. Negative slack means failure.
Metastability: when data changes right at the capture instant, the output can hover in between before settling ("What is metastability").
An 8-bit adder passes its carry (the "1" carried to the next column) through 8 stages of 0. 25 nanoseconds each, plus 0. 5 nanoseconds of flip-flop overhead.
The slowest case needs 8 times 0. 25 plus 0. 5 equals 2. 5 nanoseconds, so the safe maximum clock is 400 megahertz. At 2. 0 nanoseconds (500 megahertz) the slack is -0.
5 nanoseconds. Adding 1 + 1 still works, since its carry moves only one stage.
Adding 255 + 1 sends the carry through all 8 bits, so the top bit gets a stale carry and the answer is wrong. That is the whole idea.
"If the clock period is shorter than clock-to-Q plus the longest logic delay plus setup, flip-flops sample before data has settled: setup violations.
The longest paths fail first, so you get pattern-dependent wrong results, worse when hot or at low voltage, and possibly metastability.
Power and heat rise with frequency too, and interfaces like memory or SPI slaves have their own limits. Hold violations aren't affected by frequency.
The fix is to pipeline or optimize the critical path, raise the voltage, or lower the clock."
